title: Sticky Sessions (Session Affinity) at the Load Balancer
lesson:
Sticky sessions, also called session affinity, tell a load balancer to send every request from the same client to the same backend instance instead of spreading them freely. The balancer identifies the client with a cookie it inserts itself, a hash of the client's IP address, or an application session ID, and maps that key to one backend. Teams reach for it when servers keep per-user state in local memory, such as a login session, a shopping cart, or a warm in-process cache, and a request landing on a different instance would find none of it.

The cost is that stickiness works against the reason you load balance in the first place. Load is no longer spread per request but per client, so a few heavy users pinned to one instance can overload it while its neighbors sit idle. If a pinned instance crashes, every session held only in its memory is lost and those users are logged out or lose their carts. Scaling down and deploying get harder too, because you can't just remove an instance without either dropping its sessions or waiting for them to drain. Source-IP hashing adds its own flaws: many users behind one corporate NAT or mobile carrier gateway share an IP and all land on one backend, while a client whose IP changes mid-session gets rerouted and loses its state.

The usual fix is to make the servers stateless with respect to the session. Session data moves to a shared store such as Redis or a database, or into a signed token the client carries, so any instance can serve any request and the balancer can use plain round robin or least-connections. This restores even load spreading, lets you kill or replace instances freely, and means a crash costs a request rather than a session. The price is an extra network hop to the session store, or larger tokens, plus the need to keep that store highly available.

Sticky sessions are not always wrong. Long-lived connections like WebSockets are inherently pinned to one server for their lifetime, and affinity can improve cache hit rates when each instance caches data for the users it serves. If you do use it, treat it as a performance optimization rather than a correctness requirement: the system should still behave correctly, just slower, when a request lands on a different instance, and you should use connection draining so instances leave rotation gracefully.

questions.prompt: Which situation is the most common reason a team enables sticky sessions?
options: Backends keep per-user session state in local memory that other instances don't have
The database needs to be sharded by user ID
TLS certificates must be unique per backend
Requests need to be encrypted end to end
questions.explanation: Affinity exists so a client keeps hitting the instance that holds its in-memory state, such as a session or cart.

questions.prompt: With sticky sessions, load is distributed evenly across backends regardless of how heavy each client's usage is.
questions.explanation: Stickiness distributes load per client rather than per request, so heavy clients pinned to one instance can overload it while others stay idle.

questions.prompt: Why is source-IP-hash affinity especially problematic for users behind a large corporate NAT?
options: Their requests are encrypted and can't be hashed
Many users share one public IP, so they all hash to the same backend and create a hot spot
The load balancer can't read IPv4 addresses behind a NAT
NAT forces every request to use a new TCP connection
questions.explanation: Hashing on IP treats all users behind one address as a single client, sending all of their traffic to one instance.

questions.prompt: The common alternative to sticky sessions is to move session data into a shared store or signed token so that backends become ____ with respect to the session.
questions.explanation: When session data lives outside the instance, any backend can serve any request, so no client needs to be pinned.

questions.prompt: If a backend instance holding sticky sessions crashes, users pinned to it lose any session state that existed only in that instance's memory.
questions.explanation: Affinity does nothing to replicate state, so in-memory sessions on a crashed instance are gone unless they were stored elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Order these events for a cookie-based sticky session, earliest first.
items: Later requests carry the cookie and the balancer routes them to the same backend
The balancer picks a backend using its normal algorithm
The client's first request arrives with no affinity cookie
The balancer records the choice by setting an affinity cookie on the response
questions.explanation: The first request is balanced normally, the choice is remembered in a cookie, and subsequent requests presenting that cookie are pinned to the same backend.
